about: Gap items 94-96: Locke, Montesquieu and Rousseau's works, so the Enlightenment's influence on the two declarations runs from specific books.

events.name: Locke Publishes Two Treatises of Government
events.description: The English philosopher John Locke anonymously publishes two essays on government. The second argues that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed, and that a people may resist a ruler who breaks that trust.
events.note: Appeared in London in late 1689; the title page is dated 1690, so some references give 1690. Largely written before the Glorious Revolution (Laslett), so no link to it is claimed.
events.significance: Locke's case for natural rights and government by consent became a cornerstone of liberal political thought. American colonists drew on it in arguing against British rule, and its echoes in the Declaration of Independence made it one of the most influential political texts in English.

events.name: Montesquieu Publishes The Spirit of the Laws
events.description: The French philosopher Montesquieu publishes a vast comparative study of laws and governments. Its best-known argument is that liberty is safest when the legislative, executive and judicial powers are held by separate bodies that check one another, a principle he drew from his reading of England's constitution.
events.note: Published anonymously in Geneva in 1748; Montesquieu wrote it in France. Placed under FR for that reason.
events.significance: Montesquieu's separation of powers became a standard principle of constitution-making. The framers of the United States Constitution cited him often, and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man stated that a society without separated powers has no constitution.

events.name: Rousseau Publishes The Social Contract
events.description: The Geneva-born philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau publishes The Social Contract, which famously declares that man is born free yet everywhere is in chains. It argues that legitimate authority comes only from an agreement among citizens, guided by the general will of the people as a whole.
events.note: Printed in Amsterdam in 1762 (the Netherlands isn't in the countries table); written in France at Montmorency. Banned in Geneva and France the same year.
events.significance: Rousseau's idea of popular sovereignty, that the people as a whole are the source of legitimate law, inspired French revolutionaries and later democratic movements. His general will has also been read, more critically, as a licence to suppress dissent in the people's name.

links.why: Locke's political and philosophical writing is one of the Enlightenment's founding works.
The Declaration's natural rights and government by the consent of the governed echo Locke's argument.
One of the central works of the French Enlightenment.
The Constitution divides power among Congress, the President and the courts; Madison cited Montesquieu in defending it.
Article 16 says a society without the separation of powers has no constitution.
One of the most influential works of the French Enlightenment.
Article 6 calls law the expression of the general will, Rousseau's phrase.
